items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: An atom of carbon-14 is chemically identical to carbon-12
items.claim: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are all carbon. They have 6 protons and react chemically the same way. They differ only in the number of neutrons — and one of them (C-14) is radioactive.
items.prompt: Why does chemistry not distinguish isotopes?

options.text: Isotopes are too rare to matter
Chemistry is governed by the electron arrangement, which depends on the number of protons (atomic number) — neutrons add mass but do not affect the electron shells that control bonding
Isotopes are the same element with the same number of neutrons

items.reveal_title: Atomic number defines the element, mass number distinguishes isotopes
items.reveal:
Nuclide notation: write the mass number A (protons + neutrons) as a superscript and atomic number Z (protons) as a subscript before the symbol. C-14 has Z=6, A=14, so it has 8 neutrons.

Because electron configuration depends only on Z, all carbon isotopes share the same chemical behaviour. They differ in mass, nuclear stability, and very slightly in reaction rates (kinetic isotope effects — useful for mechanism studies).

C-14 is radioactive with a half-life of 5730 years and decays by beta emission to N-14. Its constant atmospheric concentration (produced by cosmic rays in the upper atmosphere) underwrites radiocarbon dating of organic remains up to about 50,000 years old.
items.why: Students often confuse isotopes with different elements. The proton count is what 'makes' the element; neutrons are bookkeeping for the nucleus.

items.title: Mendeleev predicted germanium 15 years before anyone made it
items.claim: In 1871 Mendeleev published predicted properties for an undiscovered element he called 'eka-silicon'. In 1886 Winkler isolated germanium. The predicted atomic mass was 72; measured 72.6. Predicted density 5.5 g/cm3; measured 5.32.
items.prompt: How could Mendeleev predict an unknown element?

options.text: He used patterns in the existing table: rows and columns of known elements bracketed each gap. An element in the silicon column, between gallium and arsenic, must have intermediate properties — and atomic mass close to the average of its neighbours
He had advance information from chemists in Germany

items.reveal:
Mendeleev's 1871 predicted properties for eka-silicon: atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5 g/cm3, grey metal, oxide formula MO2 with density ~4.7 g/cm3, chloride MCl4 boiling under 100°C.

Winkler's 1886 germanium: atomic mass 72.6, density 5.32 g/cm3, grey metal, GeO2 density 4.7 g/cm3, GeCl4 boiling at 86°C.

The match converted scepticism into acceptance. The periodic table stopped being a memorisation aid and became a predictive theory. Similar predictions held for gallium (eka-aluminium, 1875) and scandium (eka-boron, 1879).

The predictions could not have worked if the table were merely an empirical classification. The fact that it predicted real properties of unknown elements showed that something deeper was being captured.
items.why: Theories earn their keep by predicting what no one has measured yet. Mendeleev's table did this three times in 17 years.
